paragraphs.text: Ball lightning is a glowing ball that sometimes appears during thunderstorms, lasts a few seconds, and then vanishes. Nobody has yet explained it, and scientists do not agree on a theory. This article is a history that gathers 41 sightings by scientists and trained professionals, from eight countries, between 1868 and 2020.

paragraphs.text: Ball lightning appears at random, so cameras and instruments rarely catch it. One search of about 12 000 night-sky photos found only two likely events. Thousands of eyewitness reports exist, but little scientific recording does, so reports from careful, trained observers are especially valuable.

In this sample, 73 % of sightings happened during thunderstorms, and 41 % came with a lightning strike at the same moment. The cases vary so much that some are hard to fit into one model, which suggests there may be several types.

fuller.text: There are thousands of eyewitness stories, but very few camera or instrument records, and no theory that experts agree on. Catching it on purpose is nearly hopeless: one search of about 12,000 night-sky photos found only two likely cases. So the author argues that careful reports from trained observers are an especially useful kind of evidence.

fuller.text: Reported sizes ranged from 1.5 centimetres to 15 metres, with most balls under 20 centimetres. In this sample, 73 percent appeared during a thunderstorm, and 41 percent of witnesses saw a lightning strike at the same moment. The cases vary so much that some are hard to fit into one model, which has led some researchers to suspect several types of ball lightning.

fuller.text: The author also points to cases that left physical evidence, such as a tub of water that boiled, a glowing window, and a camera-recorded light pattern. The main conclusion is that well-documented sightings can guide fieldwork and help test theories. Combined with phone and webcam footage, such cases could build a shared collection against which explanations are checked.

brief.text: Ball lightning is a glowing ball of light that sometimes shows up in thunderstorms and lasts a few seconds. Thousands of people have reported it, but few cameras have caught it, and no one agrees on what causes it. Because it is so hard to catch, this history article gathers sightings by scientists and other trained observers.

Because it is so hard to catch, this history article gathers sightings by scientists and other trained observers.

brief.text: It collects 41 such reports from eight countries, from 1868 to 2020. Even these careful witnesses describe very different sizes, times and behaviours, so there may be more than one kind. The author concludes that well-recorded cases like these can guide field research and help test ideas about ball lightning.
